days.title: Enzyme Structure & Components
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define enzymes and their biological role.
  • Describe the components of an enzyme.
  • Explain the lock-and-key and induced fit models.
  • Identify the active site and substrate.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Enzyme — a biological catalyst, usually a protein.
  • Substrate — the molecule an enzyme acts on.
  • Active site — the region where the substrate binds.
  • Cofactor — non-protein helper (e.g., metal ions).
  • Coenzyme — organic helper (e.g., NAD⁺, FAD).

📚 Lesson Content

A. What Is an Enzyme?

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions by lowering activation energy. They are not consumed in the reaction.

B. Components of an Enzyme

ComponentDescription
ApoenzymeProtein portion
CofactorNon-protein helper (metal ions: Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺)
CoenzymeOrganic helper (NAD⁺, FAD, CoA)
HoloenzymeApoenzyme + cofactor/coenzyme
Active siteWhere substrate binds

C. Models of Enzyme Action

  • Lock-and-key — active site fits substrate exactly.
  • Induced fit — active site adjusts to fit substrate better.

💬 Let's Discuss

Many reactions in your body would take years to happen on their own at body temperature. Enzymes make them happen in fractions of a second. An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it speeds up a reaction without being used up, so one enzyme molecule can work on thousands of molecules per second. Most enzymes are proteins, and many have names ending in -ase (lactase, amylase, protease).

The molecule an enzyme acts on is its substrate. The substrate fits into a pocket on the enzyme called the active site, forming an enzyme–substrate complex; the reaction occurs; the products leave; and the enzyme is free to work again. The older lock-and-key model said the active site is a rigid, exact fit. The induced-fit model, now accepted, says the active site is flexible and molds itself around the substrate as it binds, like a glove tightening around a hand. This explains why enzymes are specific: lactase breaks lactose but not sucrose.

Some enzymes need helpers. The protein part alone is the apoenzyme — inactive. When it joins its non-protein helper, it becomes the active holoenzyme. Inorganic helpers such as Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Fe²⁺ are called cofactors; organic helpers, often made from vitamins, are coenzymes — for example NAD⁺ (from niacin) and FAD (from riboflavin). This is one reason vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts.

Common mistake: mixing up the enzyme and the substrate. In "lactase digests lactose," lactase (ends in -ase) is the enzyme and lactose is the substrate. People who are lactose intolerant make too little lactase.

pairs.why: An enzyme is a protein catalyst that speeds up reactions without being used up.
The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on.
The active site is the pocket where the substrate binds.
The apoenzyme is the protein portion alone.
A cofactor is an inorganic helper such as a metal ion.
A coenzyme is an organic helper, often derived from a vitamin.
Apoenzyme + helper = the complete, active holoenzyme.

scenarios.explanation: Lactose is the molecule being broken down, so it is the substrate.
Substrates bind at the active site.

scenarios.text: Zinc is required for an enzyme to work.
scenarios.explanation: Zinc is an inorganic helper — a cofactor.
NAD⁺ is an organic helper — a coenzyme.

scenarios.text: Active site adjusts shape after substrate binds.
scenarios.explanation: The active site changing shape as substrate binds is induced fit.
Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy.

questions.text: What is the protein portion of an enzyme called?
questions.explanation: The protein part of an enzyme is the apoenzyme.

questions.text: Which model describes the active site changing shape to fit the substrate?
questions.explanation: In the induced-fit model, the active site adjusts to the substrate.

questions.text: Which of the following is a coenzyme?
questions.explanation: NAD⁺ is organic (a coenzyme); the metal ions are cofactors.

takeaways: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins.
Substrates bind to the active site.
Cofactors are inorganic; coenzymes are organic.
Two models: lock-and-key and induced fit.

days.title: Enzyme Function & Factors Affecting Activity
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain how enzymes catalyze reactions.
  • Describe factors affecting enzyme activity.
  • Explain denaturation.
  • Interpret enzyme activity graphs.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Activation energy — energy needed to start a reaction.
  • Denaturation — loss of enzyme shape and function.
  • Optimal pH/temperature — conditions where enzyme works best.
  • Inhibitor — molecule that slows/prevents enzyme action.

📚 Lesson Content

A. How Enzymes Work

Enzymes lower activation energy by bringing substrates together in the correct orientation. The enzyme is not consumed.

B. Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity

FactorEffect
TemperatureActivity increases until optimum, then denatures
pHEach enzyme has an optimal pH
Substrate concentrationRate increases until saturation
Enzyme concentrationRate increases with more enzyme
InhibitorsReduce or block activity

C. Types of Inhibition

  • Competitive — inhibitor binds active site
  • Non-competitive — inhibitor binds elsewhere, changes shape

💬 Let's Discuss

Every reaction needs a small push to get started, called the activation energy — like the push needed to roll a boulder over a small hill before it can roll downhill. Enzymes lower the activation energy by holding substrates in the best position and straining their bonds. They do not change how much energy the reaction releases.

Because enzymes depend on shape, anything that changes shape changes activity. Temperature: warming increases collisions, so activity rises up to the optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes). Beyond that, bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, the active site is destroyed, and activity drops sharply — the enzyme is denatured. This is why very high fever is dangerous. pH: each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin in the acidic stomach works best at pH 2; trypsin in the small intestine works best near pH 8. Substrate concentration: more substrate increases the rate until all active sites are busy. At that point the enzyme is saturated, and adding more substrate does not help — like a jeepney that is already full.

Inhibitors slow enzymes. A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and occupies the active site; adding more substrate can outcompete it. A non-competitive inhibitor binds somewhere else (an allosteric site) and changes the enzyme's shape, so more substrate does not help. Many drugs and poisons are inhibitors: some antibiotics block bacterial enzymes, and certain pesticides block an enzyme in nerve cells.

Common mistake: saying cold temperatures denature enzymes. Cold only slows them; they recover when warmed.

pairs.why: Activation energy is the energy needed to start a reaction.
Denaturation is the loss of an enzyme's shape, so its active site fails.

pairs.right: pH where enzyme is most active
pairs.why: Each enzyme works fastest at its optimal pH.
A competitive inhibitor occupies the active site.
A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape.
Saturation means every active site is already occupied.

scenarios.text: Enzyme activity increases then drops sharply with temperature.
scenarios.explanation: Activity drops sharply above the optimum because the enzyme denatures.

scenarios.text: Stomach enzyme pepsin works best at pH 2.
scenarios.explanation: Pepsin's best pH, 2, is its optimal pH.

scenarios.text: Adding more substrate doesn't increase rate beyond a point.
scenarios.explanation: When all active sites are full, the enzyme is saturated.

scenarios.text: A molecule binds to the active site, blocking the substrate.
scenarios.explanation: Blocking the active site is competitive inhibition.

scenarios.text: A molecule binds elsewhere and changes enzyme shape.
scenarios.explanation: Binding elsewhere and changing shape is non-competitive inhibition.

scenarios.text: Enzymes lower this to speed reactions.
scenarios.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy.

questions.text: What happens to most enzymes at very high temperatures?
questions.explanation: High heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so it denatures.
A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and blocks the substrate.

questions.text: Enzyme activity stops increasing with more substrate because:
questions.explanation: Once every active site is occupied, adding substrate cannot raise the rate.

takeaways: Temperature, pH, substrate/enzyme concentration affect activity.
Two inhibition types: competitive and non-competitive.

days.title: Oxidation & Reduction Reactions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define oxidation and reduction.
  • Explain oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions.
  • Identify oxidizing and reducing agents.
  • Explain the role of electron carriers.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Oxidation — loss of electrons (LEO).
  • Reduction — gain of electrons (GER).
  • Redox reaction — coupled oxidation & reduction.
  • Electron carrier — molecule that shuttles electrons (NAD⁺, FAD).

📚 Lesson Content

A. LEO GER

  • Lose Electrons = Oxidation
  • Gain Electrons = Reduction

B. Redox in Biology

ReactionWhat Happens
NAD⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺ → NADHNAD⁺ is reduced (gains electrons)
NADH → NAD⁺ + 2e⁻ + H⁺NADH is oxidized (loses electrons)

C. Electron Carriers

  • NAD⁺/NADH — key carrier in respiration
  • FAD/FADH₂ — another carrier
  • NADP⁺/NADPH — carrier in photosynthesis

💬 Let's Discuss

Much of the energy work in living things is really the movement of electrons. When one molecule loses electrons, another must gain them. These paired reactions are called redox reactions (reduction + oxidation).

Oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons. The memory aid is LEO says GER: Lose Electrons = Oxidation, Gain Electrons = Reduction (or OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). It may seem strange that gaining something is called "reduction," but think of it as reducing the positive charge: adding a negative electron lowers it.

In biology, electrons usually travel together with hydrogen. So a molecule that loses hydrogen is usually being oxidized, and one that gains hydrogen is being reduced. Cells do not let electrons fly around freely; they use electron carriers like rechargeable batteries. NAD⁺ picks up two electrons and a hydrogen ion to become NADH (reduced, "charged"). Later, NADH gives the electrons away and becomes NAD⁺ again (oxidized, "empty"). FAD becomes FADH₂ the same way. NAD⁺ and FAD work in cellular respiration; a close relative, NADP⁺/NADPH, works in photosynthesis.

The molecule that gives away electrons is the reducing agent; the one that takes them is the oxidizing agent. Oxygen is a strong electron taker, which is why it is the final electron acceptor in respiration.

Common mistake: thinking oxidation always needs oxygen. It is defined by electrons, not by oxygen.

pairs.why: Oxidation means losing electrons (LEO).
Reduction means gaining electrons (GER).
Oxidation and reduction always occur together in a redox reaction.
NAD⁺ gains electrons and H to become NADH — reduction.
NADH gives up electrons to become NAD⁺ — oxidation.
FAD accepts electrons in respiration and becomes FADH₂.

scenarios.explanation: Losing electrons is oxidation.
Gaining electrons is reduction.
NAD⁺ gains electrons to become NADH, so it is reduced.
NADH loses electrons to become NAD⁺, so it is oxidized.
Photosynthesis uses NADP⁺/NADPH as its electron carrier.

choices.label: Lose e⁻ = oxidation; gain e⁻ = reduction
Lose e⁻ = reduction; gain e⁻ = oxidation

scenarios.explanation: LEO GER: lose electrons = oxidation, gain electrons = reduction.

questions.explanation: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.

questions.text: When NAD⁺ accepts electrons, it is:
questions.explanation: Accepting electrons means NAD⁺ is reduced.

questions.text: Which carrier is used in photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses NADP⁺; respiration uses NAD⁺ and FAD.

takeaways: Oxidation = loss of electrons; Reduction = gain of electrons.
NAD⁺/NADH and FAD/FADH₂ are key carriers in respiration.

days.title: Redox in Biological Systems
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain redox in respiration and photosynthesis.
  • Describe how electron transport chains work.
  • Relate redox to energy production.
  • Identify examples of redox in daily life.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Electron transport chain (ETC) — series of redox reactions producing ATP.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation — ATP production using ETC in respiration.
  • Photophosphorylation — ATP production using ETC in photosynthesis.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Redox in Cellular Respiration

  • Glucose is oxidized → CO₂
  • O₂ is reduced → H₂O
  • Electrons carried by NADH/FADH₂ to the ETC
  • ATP produced by chemiosmosis

B. Redox in Photosynthesis

  • H₂O is oxidized → O₂
  • CO₂ is reduced → glucose
  • Electrons carried by NADPH
  • ATP produced by photophosphorylation

C. Everyday Redox

  • Rusting of iron (oxidation)
  • Burning of fuel (oxidation)
  • Batteries (electron flow)
  • Bleaching (oxidation of pigments)

💬 Let's Discuss

Respiration and photosynthesis are giant redox processes, and they mirror each other. In cellular respiration (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy), glucose loses its hydrogens and electrons as it becomes CO₂, so glucose is oxidized. Oxygen gains those electrons and hydrogens to become water, so oxygen is reduced. In photosynthesis, the direction reverses: water is split and loses electrons (water is oxidized, releasing O₂), and CO₂ gains electrons and hydrogens to build sugar (CO₂ is reduced).

Why not release all the energy at once? Burning glucose in a fire releases it explosively as heat. Cells instead pass electrons down an electron transport chain (ETC) — a series of membrane proteins, each slightly more electron-hungry than the last — like walking down a staircase instead of jumping off a roof. At each step, a little energy is used to pump H⁺ ions across a membrane, building a gradient.

Then H⁺ ions flow back through an enzyme called ATP synthase, which spins like a water turbine and makes ATP. Using an H⁺ gradient to make ATP is called chemiosmosis. In mitochondria, when the electrons come from food and end on oxygen, it is oxidative phosphorylation. In chloroplasts, when the energy comes from light, it is photophosphorylation.

Redox happens outside cells too: rusting iron and a burning candle are oxidations. Common mistake: saying "oxygen is oxidized in respiration." Oxygen accepts electrons, so it is reduced.

pairs.why: An ETC passes electrons through a series of carriers in a membrane.
In mitochondria, ATP made using the ETC and oxygen is oxidative phosphorylation.
In chloroplasts, ATP made using light-driven ETC is photophosphorylation.
Chemiosmosis is ATP synthesis powered by H⁺ flowing through ATP synthase.
Rusting is iron losing electrons to oxygen — an oxidation.

scenarios.text: Glucose is broken down to CO₂ in respiration.
scenarios.explanation: Glucose loses electrons and hydrogen as it becomes CO₂ — it is oxidized.
O₂ gains electrons and hydrogen to form water — it is reduced.
Splitting water releases electrons and O₂ — water is oxidized.
CO₂ gains electrons to build glucose — it is reduced.

scenarios.text: Electrons pass through a series of proteins.
scenarios.explanation: Electrons passing through a series of proteins is the ETC.
Iron losing electrons to oxygen is oxidation.

questions.explanation: Glucose loses electrons in respiration, so it is oxidized.
CO₂ gains electrons and hydrogen to form sugar, so it is reduced.

questions.text: ATP production from the ETC in respiration is called:
questions.explanation: The ETC in respiration makes ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.

takeaways: Redox is the basis of energy flow in cells.
